contract_plain_english: The printed condition allows the expected degree to vanish. For example, with p(n)=n^−3 the expected degree is O(1), but the graph has no edges with probability tending to one. Its maximum degree is therefore zero with high probability, so no positive multiple of log n/log log n can be attained with probability 0.9. This obstructs the literal statement and explains the need for a positive lower bound on d.

source_evidence.observation: The source explicitly permits p to depend on n while n tends to infinity.
The literal hypothesis is only d=O(1), whereas the conclusion asks with probability 0.9 for a vertex whose degree is a positive Ω(log n/log log n).
The asserted threshold log n/log log n diverges as n tends to infinity and Ω requires a positive constant multiplier.

binders: The allowed positive connection-probability sequence p_n=n^−3.
Random graphs G_n distributed as G(n,p_n).
conclusions: The probability that G_n contains any edge is at most n(n−1)p_n/2 and therefore tends to zero.
With probability tending to one, every vertex of G_n has degree zero.
For every fixed c>0, the probability that G_n has a vertex of degree at least c log n/log log n tends to zero and is eventually less than 0.9.
Consequently, the printed assumption d=O(1) does not imply the positive Ω(log n/log log n) vertex-degree conclusion.
definitions_and_conventions: In G(n,p), every unordered pair of distinct vertices is connected independently with probability p.
The notation d=O(1) imposes an eventual upper bound but no positive lower bound.
A positive Ω(log n/log log n) degree bound requires at least one vertex of positive and eventually growing degree.
hypotheses: The sequence p_n may depend on n, as expressly allowed by the standing context.
The expected degrees satisfy d_n=(n−1)/n^3=O(1), so this family satisfies the literal hypothesis of Exercise 2.4.5.
implicit_context: The connection probability is permitted to vary with n.
The probability is taken over the random edge set.
The obstruction uses a strictly positive probability sequence, so it does not depend on whether the endpoint p=0 is admitted.

details: The choice p_n=n^−3 lies in [0,1] for positive n.
Its expected degree tends to zero while still satisfying d_n=O(1).
The expected total number of edges is n(n−1)p_n/2, which tends to zero.
Thus the graph is empty with probability tending to one.
One admissible p(n) sequence suffices to refute a conclusion asserted for the whole d=O(1) regime.
The failure holds for every positive constant hidden in the Ω notation.

undebatable_constraints: The obstruction must respect the source’s permission for p to depend on n.
The Ω multiplier must be treated as strictly positive.
The obstruction must address the existential maximum-degree event in Exercise 2.4.5.
It is enough to exhibit one admissible expected-degree sequence for which the claimed probability is eventually below 0.9.
